title: Practice Set 3 — DataFrames: The Core Abstraction
description: Apply your understanding of DataFrames by creating them from Python data and files, enforcing schemas, exploring data with show/printSchema/describe, reasoning about lazy evaluation and immutability, and building a complete read-transform-act pipeline.

datasets.description: NordGrid daily meter readings for one week across all four regions. 100 rows.

columns.name: region
columns.description: Operating region: NORTH, SOUTH, EAST, or WEST

characteristics.edgeValues: 1 row has daily_kw of 5000.0, 1 row has 9999.9

datasets.description: NordGrid substation reference table. 8 rows, two substations per region.

tasks.title: Build NordGrid's Substation Reference Table

description.context: NordGrid's SCADA team sends a list of three new wind substations that need to be added to the data platform. Before the substations are registered in the official CSV file, the data engineering team needs to create a temporary DataFrame to validate the data. The team requires an explicit schema — they never rely on Spark's type inference for reference data.
description.task: Create a DataFrame from the following Python data using spark.createDataFrame() with an explicit StructType schema. The DataFrame should have four columns: substation_id (StringType, non-nullable), name (StringType, non-nullable), capacity_mw (DoubleType, non-nullable), and region (StringType, non-nullable). Store the result in a variable called new_substations.
description.validationHint: Your DataFrame should have exactly 3 rows and 4 columns. All columns should be non-nullable. Call printSchema() to verify the types match.

tasks.partialCredit: 5 independent assertions. Each passed assertion earns 1/5 credit.

fields.label: What is the right way to build a 3-row reference DataFrame the team will trust in production?
options: spark.createDataFrame(rows, schema=StructType([...])) with every field's nullable=False
spark.createDataFrame(rows) and let Spark infer the schema — it's only 3 rows
spark.read.csv(StringIO(...), inferSchema=True) so the engine picks types
fields.correctAnswer: spark.createDataFrame(rows, schema=StructType([...])) with every field's nullable=False
fields.rationale: Reference data must use an explicit StructType — the team's policy bans inference for trusted tables. Three rows is no exception.

tasks.title: Load NordGrid Readings with an Explicit Schema

description.context: NordGrid's daily meter readings CSV has been loaded into the Bronze layer. A junior engineer's first task is to read this file into a DataFrame using an explicit schema instead of inferSchema. The team's coding standard requires explicit schemas for all production reads because inference is slow on large files and can produce wrong types.
description.task: Read the file PS3_data_readings.csv into a DataFrame using spark.read.csv() with an explicit StructType schema. Define meter_id as StringType (non-nullable), daily_kw as DoubleType (nullable), date as StringType (non-nullable), and region as StringType (non-nullable). Store the result in a variable called readings.
description.validationHint: Your DataFrame should have 100 rows and 4 columns. The daily_kw column should be DoubleType (not StringType). Check with printSchema().

tasks.partialCredit: 5 independent assertions. Each passed assertion earns 1/5 credit.

fields.label: Which read pattern matches the team's standard for production CSV ingestion?
options: spark.read.schema(StructType([...])).csv(path, header=True) — the schema fixes daily_kw as DoubleType up front
spark.read.csv(path, header=True, inferSchema=True) — convenient and fast on production files
spark.read.csv(path).toDF('meter_id','daily_kw','date','region') — typing happens later via .cast()
fields.correctAnswer: spark.read.schema(StructType([...])).csv(path, header=True) — the schema fixes daily_kw as DoubleType up front
fields.rationale: Explicit StructType is the only option that locks types before the read; inferSchema scans the file twice and may misread numeric columns as strings.

description.context: Every line of PySpark falls into one of three categories. TRANSFORMATIONS (filter, withColumn, select, join) build the plan and return a NEW DataFrame; nothing actually runs. ACTIONS (count, show, collect, write, take) trigger execution — Spark runs the entire plan from source to produce a result. METADATA-ONLY calls (printSchema, columns, explain) read information that already lives on the driver and do not touch the data at all. The trap: every action triggers a FRESH read from source by default. Calling count() then show() reads the source file TWICE unless you cache.
description.task: Classify each numbered line and predict the number of disk reads.
description.validationHint: Remember: printSchema() is neither a transformation nor an action — it reads metadata only. explain() also does not trigger execution.

evidence.label: Pipeline code
evidence.content:
df = spark.read.parquet('bronze/scada/')           # Line 1
df.printSchema()                                    # Line 2
df = df.filter(col('rpm') >= 0)                     # Line 3
df = df.filter(col('turbine_id').isNotNull())       # Line 4
print(f"Filtered count: {df.count()}")              # Line 5
df = df.withColumn('temp_f', col('temp') * 9/5 + 32) # Line 6
df.explain()                                        # Line 7
df.show(5)                                          # Line 8

fields.label: Line 1 — spark.read.parquet('bronze/scada/'): what happens?
options: Action — read.parquet() loads the entire file into the driver's memory immediately, before any filters are applied.
Transformation — read returns a DataFrame describing the plan to read; no bytes are loaded until an action triggers the plan.
Neither — this is session setup, similar to creating a SparkSession; it does not interact with data.
Action only when the file is small — Spark eagerly reads small files but lazily reads large ones.
fields.correctAnswer: Transformation — read returns a DataFrame describing the plan to read; no bytes are loaded until an action triggers the plan.
fields.rationale: spark.read is lazy like every other transformation. It returns a DataFrame object that REPRESENTS the read; no data is fetched. The most common Junior confusion is the word 'read' — in everyday English it means 'fetch now', but in Spark every operation is deferred until an action.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: read does not load to driver; even when actions run, data stays on executors.

Option C: read does interact with the data plan (it builds the read node).

Option D: Spark applies the same lazy semantics regardless of file size.

fields.label: Line 2 — df.printSchema(): does this trigger execution?
options: Yes — printSchema reads the data to confirm the actual column types match the declared schema.
No — schema is metadata stored on the driver; printSchema reads that metadata without touching any data rows.
Yes — but only a small sample (~1000 rows) of data to verify schema integrity.
Sometimes — Parquet schemas trigger execution but CSV schemas do not.
fields.correctAnswer: No — schema is metadata stored on the driver; printSchema reads that metadata without touching any data rows.
fields.rationale: Schema is held on the driver as a StructType object the moment the DataFrame is built. printSchema just formats and prints it. The most common Junior confusion is conflating printSchema with inferSchema; inference DOES read data, but printing the already-known schema does not.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Spark trusts the declared/embedded schema; it does not re-verify by scanning rows.

Option C: No sampling occurs in printSchema.

Option D: Schema-printing behavior is identical across file formats.

fields.label: Line 5 — df.count(): what happens?
options: Transformation — count appends a counting node to the plan; the actual count runs at the next action.
Action — count() triggers execution of the WHOLE plan from source through both filters, and returns the resulting row count.
Action — count counts the rows of the source file without applying the filters above; filters affect display but not count.
Neither — count is a metadata operation that reads the file's row-count statistic from Parquet metadata.
fields.correctAnswer: Action — count() triggers execution of the WHOLE plan from source through both filters, and returns the resulting row count.
fields.rationale: count is one of the canonical actions. It triggers Spark to execute the entire plan: read parquet, apply filter for rpm >= 0, apply filter for not-null turbine_id, then count. The most common Junior confusion is thinking count uses Parquet's pre-computed row stats; that only works when there are no filters, and once filters are in the plan Spark must actually execute them.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: count is an ACTION, not a transformation.

Option C: count respects the entire plan; filters are applied before counting.

Option D: Parquet metadata count is bypassed once filters are added.

fields.label: Line 7 — df.explain(): does this trigger execution?
options: Yes — explain runs the plan to capture timing data so it can show real performance.
No — explain prints the plan as text by walking the in-memory plan tree on the driver; no data is processed.
Yes — but only the Catalyst optimization phase runs, not the actual execution.
Yes for explain(True), no for explain() — the True flag triggers data sampling.
fields.correctAnswer: No — explain prints the plan as text by walking the in-memory plan tree on the driver; no data is processed.
fields.rationale: explain is a debugging primitive: it serializes the plan tree to a string. The Catalyst phases (Parsed, Analyzed, Optimized) all run on the driver during plan construction, not at explain time. The most common Junior confusion is thinking explain runs anything; in fact explain is the ONLY way to inspect Spark's plan WITHOUT triggering execution.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: No timing data is collected; explain shows the static plan.

Option C: Catalyst phases run during plan construction, not at explain time.

Option D: explain(True) prints more detail; neither variant samples data.

fields.label: How many times does Spark read the source Parquet file from disk during the entire script?
fields.rationale: Two actions trigger execution: count() on line 5 reads the file and applies filters to count rows. show(5) on line 8 reads the file again and applies all transformations (filters + withColumn) to display 5 rows. printSchema() and explain() do not read data. Each action triggers a fresh execution of the plan from source.

tasks.title: Explore NordGrid's Meter Quality Profile

description.context: NordGrid's data quality team has received a new batch of meter readings and needs a quick profile before the Bronze-to-Silver pipeline runs. The engineer must check the schema, view sample rows, and compute summary statistics to identify potential data quality issues — null values, negative readings, and unexpected extremes.
description.task: Load PS3_data_readings.csv into a DataFrame called readings (using header=True and inferSchema=True for quick exploration). Then use the three exploration methods to answer three questions: (1) store the result of printSchema() as a string using readings._jdf.schema().treeString() in a variable called schema_str, (2) store the row count in a variable called row_count, and (3) store the result of describe() on the daily_kw column in a variable called kw_stats.
description.validationHint: row_count should be 100. kw_stats should be a DataFrame with 5 rows (count, mean, stddev, min, max). The count in describe() will show how many non-null values exist — compare this to the row count to spot nulls.

tasks.partialCredit: 4 independent assertions. Each passed assertion earns 1/4 credit.

fields.label: Which trio of methods gives the quickest data-quality profile of a fresh Bronze CSV?
options: printSchema() for column types, count() for row total, describe('daily_kw') for min/max/mean/stddev/non-null count
show(5), collect(), and toPandas() — collect every row to the driver and inspect it
explain(), cache(), and persist() — these reveal the read plan and warm the cache
fields.correctAnswer: printSchema() for column types, count() for row total, describe('daily_kw') for min/max/mean/stddev/non-null count
fields.rationale: printSchema/count/describe form the canonical 'first look' triad. collect() pulls everything to the driver and explain() reveals the plan, not the data.

description.context: DataFrames have three load-bearing properties that drive Spark's design. DISTRIBUTED: rows are scattered across executors, never one big in-memory collection. TYPED: every column has a known type, validated at plan time, not at row scan time. IMMUTABLE: transformations return NEW DataFrames; the original is never modified. The variable reassignment pattern (df = df.filter(...)) LOOKS like mutation but is actually 'point the name df at a new DataFrame'. Immutability is what makes failure recovery safe — if a task crashes mid-transformation, Spark can re-run it from scratch because the input data is guaranteed unchanged.
description.task: Decide which statements are true and why.
description.validationHint: Think carefully about what immutability means for variable reassignment — the variable changes, but does the DataFrame?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content: Four statements about DataFrame properties; classify each.

fields.label: Statement: 'When you call df = df.filter(col("daily_kw") > 0), Spark modifies the original DataFrame by removing rows with non-positive values.'
options: True — Spark mutates the DataFrame in place; the rows are physically removed from the existing object.
False — DataFrames are immutable; filter() returns a NEW DataFrame, and the assignment rebinds the name df to that new object while the original is garbage-collected.
True — but only when the filter returns at least one row; empty results trigger immutable behavior.
Partly true — the LOGICAL DataFrame is new but the underlying storage is mutated for efficiency.
fields.correctAnswer: False — DataFrames are immutable; filter() returns a NEW DataFrame, and the assignment rebinds the name df to that new object while the original is garbage-collected.
fields.rationale: Every Spark transformation returns a new DataFrame. The reassignment `df = df.filter(...)` creates a new object and points the name `df` at it; the old DataFrame is unreferenced and gets cleaned up. The most common Junior confusion is reading the code as mutation because the SYNTAX looks like Pandas/SQL mutation; in Spark, the same syntax is rebinding.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Spark never mutates DataFrames; this is a foundational invariant.

Option C: Behavior is identical regardless of result size.

Option D: Both the logical and physical layers are immutable; storage is also append-only.

fields.label: Statement: 'When you read a CSV with inferSchema=True, Spark scans the data to guess column types. This is slower than providing an explicit StructType schema.'
options: True — inferSchema makes Spark do an EXTRA full pass over the file just to determine types, which doubles read time on large files.
False — Spark uses the column NAMES in the header row to guess types instantly; inferSchema and explicit schema take the same time.
False — inferSchema reads only the first 1000 rows, so it is actually FASTER than schema validation.
True — but only for very small files; on large files the JIT optimizer makes inferSchema and explicit schema equivalent.
fields.correctAnswer: True — inferSchema makes Spark do an EXTRA full pass over the file just to determine types, which doubles read time on large files.
fields.rationale: CSV is schemaless on disk, so inferSchema requires Spark to scan every row, examine each value, and pick a compatible type per column — effectively two reads (one for inference, one for the actual data load). An explicit StructType skips inference entirely. The most common Junior confusion is treating inferSchema as 'free convenience'; in production it is an expensive default.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Header rows contain names, not types; type inference requires reading values.

Option C: Sampling is unsafe (it can miss types) and Spark scans all rows by default.

Option D: Performance gap holds at all file sizes; the JIT does not eliminate the extra read.

fields.label: Statement: 'printSchema() and describe() are both actions — they both trigger execution of the plan and move data across the cluster.'
options: True — both methods produce output by reading data; output cannot exist without execution.
False — printSchema() reads the schema metadata on the driver without execution; describe() IS an action that scans all data to compute count/mean/stddev/min/max.
True — but only describe() shuffles; printSchema reads from one executor.
False — neither is an action; both read driver-side metadata.
fields.correctAnswer: False — printSchema() reads the schema metadata on the driver without execution; describe() IS an action that scans all data to compute count/mean/stddev/min/max.
fields.rationale: Lumping these together is the trap. printSchema is metadata-only (driver-side, instant). describe must scan every row across all executors to compute statistics — full action with shuffle. The most common Junior confusion is treating any method that prints output as an action; in reality printSchema is one of the few exceptions that prints WITHOUT running the plan.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: printSchema produces output from metadata, not from row scans.

Option C: printSchema does not touch executors at all.

Option D: describe is genuinely an action; lumping with printSchema is wrong.

fields.label: Statement: 'Immutability makes distributed processing safe because if an executor fails during a transformation, Spark can retry the task without worrying about corrupted data.'
options: True — because transformations never modify the source partitions, Spark can re-run any failed task from clean input data; immutability is the foundation of fault tolerance.
False — Spark relies on checkpointing (writing intermediate state to disk) for fault tolerance; immutability is unrelated to retries.
True — but only at Stage 1; later stages depend on shuffle output and need separate fault tolerance.
False — immutability is a programming-model convenience; retries are handled by external coordinators like YARN.
fields.correctAnswer: True — because transformations never modify the source partitions, Spark can re-run any failed task from clean input data; immutability is the foundation of fault tolerance.
fields.rationale: Immutability + lineage (the recorded plan) = fault tolerance. If task N on executor X fails, Spark looks at the input partition (still intact, immutable) and the recorded transformation (still intact in the plan) and re-runs it on another executor. The most common Junior confusion is overrating checkpointing; checkpointing is for cutting long lineages, not the primary fault-tolerance mechanism.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Checkpointing is an optimization, not the foundation; the foundation is immutability + lineage.

Option C: All stages benefit from immutability; shuffle output is also immutable.

Option D: YARN allocates resources; Spark itself handles task retries via lineage.

tasks.title: Build NordGrid's Meter Validation Pipeline

description.context: NordGrid's data engineering team needs a validation pipeline that reads raw meter readings from the Bronze layer, removes invalid data, and writes clean output. The pipeline must handle three data quality issues present in the dataset: null daily_kw values (sensor malfunctions), negative daily_kw values (faulty sensors), and readings with daily_kw of exactly 0.0 (meters that reported but measured nothing — these are valid and should be kept).
description.task: Write a complete pipeline that: (1) reads PS3_data_readings.csv with an explicit StructType schema defining meter_id as StringType, daily_kw as DoubleType (nullable), date as StringType, and region as StringType; (2) filters out rows where daily_kw is null; (3) filters out rows where daily_kw is negative (but keeps rows where daily_kw is exactly 0.0); (4) stores the final result in a variable called clean_readings. Follow the variable reassignment pattern — use the same variable name df for each transformation step.
description.validationHint: The raw dataset has 100 rows: 7 nulls and 4 negatives should be removed. Zero-value readings (2 rows) should remain. Your result should have 89 rows.

tasks.partialCredit: 6 independent assertions. Each passed assertion earns 1/6 credit.

conceptsCombined: Reading CSV with explicit StructType schema (Lessons 3-4)
Filtering with col() expressions (Lesson 8, previewing Module 4)
Lazy evaluation — all transformations build a plan, verification triggers execution (Lesson 5)
synthesisNotes.rationale: This task mirrors NordGrid's actual Bronze-to-Silver validation step. The student must combine schema enforcement, null handling, conditional filtering (negative vs zero edge case), and the read-transform-act pattern from Lesson 10. The zero-value edge case tests whether the student uses >= 0 (wrong — keeps negatives if misread) vs > 0 (wrong — removes zeros) vs the correct two-step approach.

fields.label: Validation pipeline must drop nulls and negatives but KEEP zero readings. Which filter chain is correct?
options: df.filter(col('daily_kw').isNotNull()).filter(col('daily_kw') >= 0)
df.filter(col('daily_kw') > 0) — single filter, faster, and zero is invalid anyway
df.na.drop().filter(col('daily_kw') != 0) — drop any null row then exclude zeros
fields.rationale: `>= 0` keeps zero (a meter that reported but measured nothing) while excluding negatives; `> 0` would silently drop valid zero readings.

selfCheck.foundationModuleException: Not applicable — Module 3 is Core Mechanics phase. Task mix is write-the-code dominant (3 of 6) per §2.4 junior Core Mechanics guidance.
selfCheck.theoryPracticeBoundary: Theory examples use meters with the standard schema. Task 1 uses substation reference data instead (same StructType pattern, different entity). Task 6 uses the same meter data but with a different filtering requirement (preserve zero-value readings) not shown in the theory's examples, testing transfer of the filter concept.
selfCheck.datasetNotes: PS3_data_readings.csv has 100 rows with intentional quality issues (7 nulls, 4 negatives, 2 zeros, 2 extreme values). The zero-value edge case in Task 6 is the key differentiator — students who blindly filter daily_kw > 0 (as shown in the theory) will lose the 2 valid zero readings.
